analysis.one_liner: Gives permanent legal status to young immigrants brought to the U.S. as children who meet work, school, or service requirements.
analysis.headline: The Dream Act of 2025 was introduced in the Senate on December 4, 2025, with bipartisan sponsorship, and has been referred to the Judiciary Committee with no further action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill lets certain immigrants who entered the United States as children — including current DACA recipients — apply to stay permanently. They first get an 8-year conditional green card, then can remove the conditions by finishing college (two years), serving in the military (two years), or working steadily (three of the years they held work authorization). People with serious criminal records are excluded, and applicants must pass background checks, pay a fee (waived for children, students in extreme poverty, or those facing homelessness, disability, or major medical debt), and clear any unpaid federal taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the population of young undocumented immigrants often called Dreamers — people brought to the U.S. as children, long-term residents under 18 at entry, current DACA recipients, and some others in protected statuses. The bill gives them protection from deportation, work authorization, and a path to lawful permanent residence and eventual citizenship. Their families, employers, and communities also gain stability.

how_it_helps.text: DACA recipients are automatically eligible for a conditional green card unless they have since engaged in conduct that would disqualify them from DACA.

Applicants get an 8-year conditional permanent residence, protection from deportation while their application is pending, and work authorization; school-aged children who meet the requirements get a stay of removal and a work permit.

Conditions are removed — making status permanent and opening a path to naturalization — after two years of college, two years of military service with honorable discharge, or employment in at least three of the years with valid work authorization; hardship, disability, and caregiving exceptions apply.
Information in applications cannot be used for immigration enforcement, and applicants cannot be referred to ICE or Border Protection, which protects people who apply from being targeted.
There is no numerical cap on how many people can qualify, and fees are waived for children, extremely low-income applicants, those who are homeless or disabled, and those with large medical debts.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the processing of applications (through fees where possible), and opponents contend it rewards unlawful entry and could encourage future illegal immigration. Immigrants who had Temporary Protected Status and then lose their new status may not be able to return to TPS. Employers and agencies bear costs of new documentation and verification.

drawbacks.text: There is no numerical limit on how many people can qualify, so the fiscal and administrative costs depend entirely on demand, which critics of past versions of the bill have argued is hard to predict.

Eligibility is broad beyond DACA: it also covers people currently in Temporary Protected Status and children of certain temporary visa holders, not just those who arrived as children and grew up here.

Applicants must swear they have no unresolved federal tax debt or have entered an approved plan to pay it, and they must pay a processing fee unless they qualify for one of several narrow exemptions — real hurdles for the poorest applicants.

An alien whose conditional status expires, is terminated, or whose application is denied generally returns to whatever status they had before — which for some TPS holders may no longer exist if the designation has been terminated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it covers, the bill converts years of legal limbo into a workable path to permanent residence and citizenship, with serious screening (background checks, medical exams, tax compliance) built in and no cap on numbers. The main honest objections are that eligibility extends beyond those who arrived as small children, that there is no limit on total numbers, and that opponents argue any legalization encourages future unlawful entry. The bill's phased structure — eight conditional years with work, school, or military requirements before permanent status — addresses some of those concerns but doesn't eliminate the underlying disagreement about whether people who entered unlawfully should ever get legal status.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has not acted on it; no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin (D-IL) introduced the bill on December 4, 2025, joined by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), the bill's one cosponsor.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history as of the record provided.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: Dreamers remain in legal limbo, and the immigration enforcement and detention industries keep operating under current policy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dreamers stay in limbo; enforcement industry unaffected

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Dream Act of 2025 in the Senate on December 4, 2025.

for.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship — a Democrat leading with one Republican cosponsor — but no committee or floor votes have occurred yet, so the partisan shape of opposition is not yet visible in the record.

industries.industry: Immigration enforcement, detention, and border-security contractors
industries.note: A large share of potential applicants would gain protection from deportation and work authorization, shrinking the population subject to detention and removal services that private contractors provide. The bill expressly bars referring applicants to ICE or Border Protection.

industries.industry: Employers of immigrant workers (agriculture, construction, hospitality, care work)
industries.note: Employers in industries that rely on this workforce gain a legal, stable labor supply instead of workers facing deportation.
College enrollment or degree completion is one of the main routes to permanent status, and admitted students qualify for the initial conditional status, adding potential students.
Military service is an alternative route to permanent status, giving recruiters an additional incentive pathway for enlistment.

analysis.trajectory: The Dream Act has been introduced in many consecutive Congresses without becoming law, and this version sits in the Senate Judiciary Committee with a single cosponsor and no scheduled action. With divided control of Congress, the realistic path is that it stays in committee unless it is attached to a larger immigration or must-pass package, or public pressure produces a hearing and markup — neither of which is currently indicated in the record.
